title: The World Cup Nobody in India Can Watch
excerpt: A broadcasting deadlock leaves 1.4 billion fans in the dark—but for NRIs abroad, this could be the most accessible tournament yet
body:
## A Tournament Without a Screen

When the FIFA World Cup kicks off in the United States on June 11, India will be conspicuously absent—not merely from the pitch, where the men's national team fell short in the 2025 qualifiers, but from the airwaves. With barely three weeks to go before the biggest sporting event on the planet, no Indian broadcaster has secured the rights to televise the 104-match tournament. For a country of 1.4 billion people and a rapidly growing football fanbase, the silence is deafening.

The standoff between FIFA and India's media giants has turned what should be a month-long festival of sport into a cautionary tale about the economics of global broadcasting rights—and an unexpected windfall for the Indian diaspora, who find themselves better positioned to watch the tournament than their friends and family back home.

## The $100 Million Impasse

The root of the crisis is price. FIFA reportedly sought roughly $100 million for Indian broadcasting rights to the expanded 48-team tournament, which will be held across 16 stadiums in the US, Canada and Mexico from June 11 to July 19. India's largest sports broadcaster, JioCinema (now JioStar after the Viacom18-Star India merger), reportedly offered just $20 million—a sum FIFA dismissed out of hand. Sony, the other serious contender, has been locked in negotiations that sources say stalled in the $35-60 million range.

The mismatch reflects a fundamental disagreement about what Indian football viewership is worth. India's men's team did not qualify, which dampens casual interest. Yet FIFA's asking price assumes the subcontinent's sheer population will deliver eyeballs regardless. Indian broadcasters, burned by expensive cricket rights and a still-maturing football market, are unwilling to bet on that calculus.

The impasse has drawn judicial attention. The Delhi High Court recently issued a notice to Prasar Bharati, the state broadcaster, demanding a response on a public-interest petition that invoked the Sports Broadcasting Signals (Mandatory Sharing with Prasar Bharati) Act. The law requires that "sporting events of national importance" be made available on free-to-air channels. Whether the World Cup qualifies when India is not competing remains a live legal question. Doordarshan's DD Sports channel has emerged as a potential fallback for select marquee matches via the Free Dish platform, but a comprehensive deal remains elusive.

## The NRI Advantage

Ironically, the diaspora that The Videshi serves is far better off. In the United States, FOX holds rights to 70 matches and Telemundo will broadcast 92 in Spanish, with Peacock streaming the Spanish-language feed. In the United Kingdom, BBC iPlayer offers free coverage—a rarity for a major football tournament. Australia's SBS will carry matches free-to-air, and Bell Media has secured Canadian rights.

Match scheduling further tilts the balance. With games in American prime time, kick-offs will fall between roughly 1:30 AM and 9:30 AM IST—punishing hours for viewers in Mumbai or Delhi, but perfectly civilised for fans in New York, London or Sydney. For the first time, NRIs will not need to set 3 AM alarms; the World Cup is coming to their time zone.

FIFA's own streaming platform, FIFA+, may offer some coverage in markets without a broadcast partner, though the extent of its India offering remains unclear. Predictably, VPN services have seen a surge in Indian search traffic as fans explore workarounds to access foreign streams—a grey area that underscores the absurdity of the current impasse.

## What the Deadlock Means for Indian Football

The broadcasting blackout is more than an inconvenience; it is a setback for the sport's development in India. Football's domestic growth—driven by the Indian Super League, English Premier League viewership and the 2023 U-17 Women's World Cup hosted in India—depends on sustained exposure to the global game. A generation of young fans who discovered football through Lionel Messi's 2022 triumph in Qatar may find themselves locked out of the sequel.

For the diaspora, the situation carries a bittersweet irony. NRIs have long complained about being afterthoughts in Indian sports broadcasting, forced to navigate geo-blocks and dodgy streams to watch IPL matches. Now, as India's domestic audience faces a blackout, the tables have turned. Diaspora fans can watch every match in high definition, in their local language, at a reasonable hour.

## The Clock Is Ticking

With the opening match between Mexico and the United States at SoFi Stadium barely three weeks away, a last-minute deal remains possible. FIFA has historically resolved broadcasting disputes close to kick-off, and the reputational cost of leaving its second-largest potential market in the dark provides a powerful incentive. But each passing day without an agreement makes an ad-hoc arrangement with Doordarshan—covering only a handful of matches rather than the full 104—more likely.

For NRIs, the advice is simple: check your local listings, download your broadcaster's app, and enjoy the rare luxury of being the best-served Indian football fans on the planet. For everyone back home, the wait continues—and the frustration mounts.

nri_angle: NRIs abroad have better access to World Cup 2026 than fans in India due to the broadcasting deadlock. US, UK, Canada and Australia all have confirmed broadcasters with matches in local prime time, while India faces a potential blackout. VPNs and FIFA+ offer workarounds. The role reversal—diaspora fans well-served while India is locked out—highlights longstanding inequities in sports broadcasting access.
